column4: Multi-signal machine fingerprint library with tolerance for small changes (Windows + Linux/Docker)
column8: A machine-bound licence needs a stable fingerprint. PEMS is .NET only and also ships a Docker option.
column9: Signals: motherboard UUID, CPU id, system disk serial, physical MACs, Windows MachineGuid, /etc/machine-id; weighted with a tolerance threshold (replacing one disk or NIC is allowed, three or more changed signals invalidates the licence).
column10: Test: the same machine after reboot and one NIC replaced stays valid; another machine is invalid; output is hashed (no raw serials exposed).

column4: Install ID and install seal: install time, install key, state counter in DB and protected file
column8: Owner need: lock to the machine and to the install time. A random Install ID is created on first run and sealed with a local key (DPAPI/TPM where available); the licence binds to this ID and the fingerprint.
column9: Generate an install key pair, store the private key non-exportable (DPAPI machine scope or TPM), write the seal in two independent places (DB + file) and verify consistency on every start.
column10: Copying a disk/image to other hardware cannot open the seal (machine-bound key) and the app drops to 'activation required'.

column4: Activation request file (.pemsreq): generated on the customer server and returned to us
column8: Owner's process: a file is generated on the customer server, returned to us, then the real licence is issued and delivered. Copying only a fingerprint is not enough; a full request contract is needed.
column9: File contents: hashed fingerprint, Install ID, install time, product version, customer/order id, random nonce, signature by the install key. The customer generates and downloads it from the licence page. Everything in this flow is done in the UI; no terminal or CLI step is required (a CLI may exist only as an optional extra).
column10: Changing one byte of the request file makes the vendor tool reject it; every request has a unique nonce; the customer produces the file entirely in the browser UI.

column4: Signed licence file format (.pemslic): Ed25519/ECDSA with fields bound to the request
column8: Public key in the app, private key only at the vendor (Ed25519 offline licensing is proven).
column9: Fields: customer, Install ID, fingerprint hash, edition, modules/features, limits (sites and modules; no user limit), type and period, updates-until date (maintenance period, see CV_UPDENT), request nonce, issue counter; support a zip bundle of several licences.
column10: A licence issued for request A is never valid on install B; a tampered signature test is rejected.

column4: Licence types: lifetime, term (time period with start and end date), trial, demo

column9: Each type has its own validity logic: term = start and end date checked against a tamper-guarded clock (L_CLOCK); lifetime = no expiry; warning before expiry for term licences.
column10: Boundary tests: expiry at Jalali midnight, renewal before/after expiry, lifetime shows no expiry warning, a trial cannot be extended without a new licence.

column4: Multiple verification points (start, periodic, sensitive operations) instead of one central 'if'
column8: An ordinary attacker patches one condition; several independent checks with different consequences are needed.
column9: Checks at startup, in middleware, in a periodic Hangfire job and when publishing a module or enabling a feature; failure means read-only restricted mode, not a crash.
column10: Disabling one check does not bypass the others (internal penetration test).

column4: Anti-clone: detect snapshot/image restore and simultaneous running on two machines
column8: The scenario the owner described: a full machine image brought up elsewhere. Different hardware fails the fingerprint and machine-bound seal; restoring on the same hardware or an identical VM needs a monotonic counter and lifecycle trail.
column9: Monotonic counter in the seal plus a hash chain of the audit log; each start raises the counter; a counter lower than recorded means suspected restore; log the event and require re-activation.
column10: Documented test scenarios: (1) image on different hardware: rejected; (2) cloned VM: detected through the virtual TPM/hypervisor identifier where available, otherwise by the restore-detection counter, with the EULA clause as backstop; (3) restore from an old snapshot: warning and re-activation.

column4: Design and decision for the vendor-assisted admin password reset by file exchange (request file out, signed response file back), separate reset key, and AFTA compatibility check
column8: A customer whose production server is offline must be able to recover a lost administrator password with the vendor's help, without a back door in the product and without any remote access. The licence flow already proves that file exchange works offline; the reset reuses its shape with its own key. Gate: this row can start only after #342 (licence flow end to end) is Done. Independent of the separate administrator-recovery work done by Saber (second-admin reset, one-time recovery codes, server-side break-glass, shared audit/notification/session revocation): that work does not wait for the licence flow and this row does not block it; this flow plugs into it as the optional vendor-assisted recovery path, which must stay off until the customer enables it. 2026-10-28 plan audit: dependency/milestone corrected (see docs/audits/2026-10-28-dynamic-restful-audit.md).
column9: Write docs/design/ADMIN_RESET.md (no secrets). Flow (same shape as licence activation, all in the browser UI; no terminal or CLI step): 1) the customer opens the administrator recovery page on their installation and downloads a reset request file (.pemsrstreq: Install ID, fingerprint hash, licence id, product version, account, random nonce kept server-side as a pending request, signed by the install key); 2) the customer sends the file to us; 3) in the developer/owner UI we upload it, the tool verifies the signature, matches it to the customer and licence in the ledger, we confirm the customer, enter the reason and the identity check, and download a reset response file (.pemsreset) signed with the separate reset key and bound to the request nonce, licence id, Install ID, purpose and expiry; 4) the customer uploads the response file on the same page and the password reset form opens; the pending request is consumed so the file works once. Decide: reset-key custody. Decided 2026-10-25 by the owners: the licence key and the reset key are each created and used only on the owner computers (the own computers of Hamid and Saber, who are the owners and the developers; also called developer-local or owner machines), as the last step of the licence and reset flows. Neither key is ever in the assistant's environment, on a shared or CI server, or in the repository. The reset key is still a different key from the licence key. To settle in the ADR: whether the keys stay offline (encrypted external drive) between uses, where the backup copies are and who holds them, what the reset changes (password; MFA/passkeys and sessions as in the shared recovery rules), expiry of the response file, rate limits, audit on both sides, behaviour on a cloned or re-hosted machine (#104, #116). AFTA check (to be confirmed with the testing lab through #184): no default, master or hard-coded password and no standing vendor credential; the vendor can act only on a request that the installation itself generated, for one installation, once and for a short time; the capability is off by default and enabled explicitly by the customer administrator; every use is audited, all administrators are notified, the account sessions are revoked and the event goes to the SIEM feed; the reset key is separate from the licence key and can be revoked through an update; everything works offline by file exchange, so no remote access to the customer server is ever needed. Validity: the response file expires after a period the owner chooses in the developer UI when the file is issued: default 1 day, allowed range 1 to 7 days in whole days, and no unlimited or open-ended option (the tool refuses values outside the range and the product checks the limits again, so a correctly signed file with a longer validity is rejected). The pending reset request on the customer side expires on the same bounds. AFTA: a short, bounded, single-use validity fits the check recorded here; the 1-day default and the 7-day maximum are to be confirmed with the testing lab (#184), and if the lab wants a shorter maximum the limits change in one setting without changing the file format.
column10: Done when: an approved ADR with the file formats' fields, the key-custody details on the owner computers, the threat model (replay, wrong customer, tampered or forged file, cloned machine, clock change, leaked file) and a written AFTA compatibility assessment accepted by the security consultant; #344-#349 are written against it. The validity rule (default 1 day, range 1 to 7 days, no unlimited option) is confirmed by the AFTA assessment.

column4: Customer UI: administrator recovery page (download reset request file, upload reset response file, open the reset form), one-time, licence-bound, off by default

Gate: this row can start only after #342 (licence flow end to end) is Done. column4: CI and branch policy: pipelines run only on pushes to demo and staging (none on main or working branches), staging environment and subdomain, deployment README, dev branch retired

column11: 2026-10-25: no workflow runs on main or working branches (build.yml manual); reusable deploy-site.yml called by deploy-demo.yml and deploy-staging.yml; env/staging files; staging branch created from main+dev+demo; dev merged into main and deleted; docs/deployment/DEPLOYMENT_README.md. Staging run 40208748572 green: HTTP 200, database up to date, upload of changed files only (33.8 MB). column4: Environment data package: export the current database as a versioned, hashed, importable package and import it from the admin UI (with the existing Excel importers alongside), role-protected
column8: The application has no database export or import of its own data (only the Import Center for Excel files and the Database Update page for schema). Demo and staging need a repeatable way to capture and restore their data.
column9: Design first (ADR): logical export of every user table to a package (.pemsdata, zip) with a manifest: format version, product version, last applied migration, schema fingerprint, per-table row counts and SHA-256, package hash; import = precheck (hash, format, schema compatibility) then replace. Admin UI page for the proper role/permission only; the same page links to the Import Center for Excel imports. Disabled by setting outside demo/staging unless the owner enables it. Audit every export and import.
column10: Done when: an authorised administrator exports a package from the UI and re-imports it into an empty or existing database of the same version; a tampered or incompatible package is rejected with the reason; every action is audited; tests cover precheck, hash, round trip and the permission.

column4: Reset on deploy for demo and staging: a baseline data package shipped with the branch is applied after a version-compatibility precheck, from the UI or automatically when a new baseline arrives
column8: Row #141 asks for a nightly and an admin reset but nothing exists; a push to demo or staging updates code and schema only, data is never reset.
column9: Use the package from #352. A baseline package committed to the demo/staging overlay is uploaded by the pipeline; on first start after deploy the app compares the baseline hash with the one recorded in the database, runs the precheck and, if it passes and the environment setting allows it, resets the database to the baseline; otherwise it reports why in the admin UI. Admin UI offers the same reset by upload. Owners and developers only.
column10: Done when: pushing a new baseline to demo (and to staging) resets that environment once; an incompatible baseline leaves data untouched and shows the reason; a manual reset by upload works in the UI; tests cover both paths.

column4: Move the EF Core migrations into their own assembly (PEMS.Migrations) so PEMS.Persistence.dll changes, and is deployed, only when its own code changes

column9: Follow the EF Core guidance for a separate migrations project: new project PEMS.Migrations (references PEMS.Persistence) holds the migration files, the snapshot and the design-time factory; the context defaults its MigrationsAssembly to it so hosts, tests and tools find the migrations; Web and Tests reference the project; update the CI drift gate, deploy script, Dockerfile, solution and every documented dotnet ef command.

column4: Field validation catalog: for every field type the constraints (required, range, length, decimals, size, count, pattern, date window, membership, uniqueness), their defaults, hard versus advisory, and the stored validation object
column8: Validation in PEMS today is thin and scattered: 260 entities but only 26 [Required] and 45 [MaxLength] attributes in 28 files, no [Range], [StringLength] or regular-expression rule anywhere, no validation library, ModelState.IsValid is checked in 8 controllers, and 64 of 65 plain text inputs in the views have no maxlength. Dynamic forms need one declarative description of the rules per field type before any engine or UI is built. Rule-builder row #46 covers user-defined rules; this row defines the built-in constraints every type carries. 2026-10-28 plan audit: dependency/milestone corrected (see docs/audits/2026-10-28-dynamic-restful-audit.md).
column9: 1) For every type in #11 list its constraints. Text: required, min/max length, pattern (named presets: code, e-mail, phone, national id), allowed characters, allow digits. Number/decimal/money: min, max, strict range, step, integer only, allow negative, allow zero, scale and precision. Date/date-time: min/max date, relative window (not in the past, not in the future, within N days), Jalali-aware, time zone. Boolean: must be true. Select/multi-select: membership, min/max selected. Lookup/user: existence, active only, scope. File/image: max size per file and in total, count, extensions, MIME, dimensions. Rich text: max length of the text after sanitisation. JSON: schema. Computed/auto-number: read-only. 2) For each constraint: default, hard (blocks the save) or advisory (hint only), message key (fa/en) and parameters. 3) Define the versioned validation object stored in the metadata registry and which constraints the physical column must also enforce (length, precision, scale) so metadata and storage cannot disagree. 4) Cross-field and semantic rules (end after start, total equals sum) use the rule builder of #46 and the expression engine of #15. 5) Persian/Arabic digit normalisation and decimal separator rules (see #364). 6) Write docs/architecture/FIELD_VALIDATION_CATALOG.md and an ADR. Best-practice sources to apply: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (allowlist, syntactic and semantic checks, server-side authority, canonicalisation, limits before parsing, safe regular expressions); Microsoft Learn ASP.NET Core model validation; WCAG 2.2 success criteria 3.3.1 and 3.3.3; RFC 9457 problem details.
column10: Done when: the catalog lists every field type of #11 with its constraints, defaults, hard or advisory flag and message keys; the rule that derives column size and precision from the constraints is decided; the PM reviewed it; rows #356-#365 reference it.

column4: Server-side validation engine: one type-dispatched validator used by every write path (forms, API, import, bulk, static modules), full list of field errors, create versus partial-update modes, localised messages
column8: A direct API call, an import or a bulk write bypasses whatever the page checks, and PEMS has no single validator to call. Validation must be authoritative on the server; the client only improves feedback.
column9: 1) Check libraries first (FluentValidation, JSON-schema validators) and record the licence in row L_OSS; custom code only with a stated reason. 2) Implement a validator in the engine layer with a dispatch table by field type (a new constraint is a new case, never a second parallel function): input = field descriptors + record + mode; create requires every required field, update checks only the keys present so an omitted key never means 'clear it'. Whitespace-only text counts as empty for required. 3) Return all violations (field, constraint code, message key, parameters), not only the first, capped by a setting (ASP.NET Core defaults to 200 errors and depth 32; set explicit limits). 4) Call it from one place in the generic CRUD pipeline and from static modules through an adapter (DataAnnotations and IValidatableObject keep working). 5) Messages resolved through the localisation resources (fa/en). 6) Validation never replaces authorisation, parameterised queries, output encoding or HTML sanitisation (OWASP). 7) Unit tests per type and constraint. Best-practice sources to apply: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (allowlist, syntactic and semantic checks, server-side authority, canonicalisation, limits before parsing, safe regular expressions); Microsoft Learn ASP.NET Core model validation; WCAG 2.2 success criteria 3.3.1 and 3.3.3; RFC 9457 problem details.
column10: Done when: every write path of the generic engine calls the validator; a request that bypasses the UI is rejected with the full error list; partial updates never clear omitted fields; messages come in the user's language; the error and depth limits are settings; tests cover each type.

column4: Client input shaping and accessible inline validation from the same constraint descriptor: maxlength/min/max/step/pattern attributes, keystroke sanitising (Persian digits, decimals, thousands separators, RTL), counters, error text with suggestion, focus first error, advisory hints
column8: Text and number inputs are hand-written per page (2,587 hand-written inputs in the audit) and carry no constraints. The component library needs one way to turn the constraint descriptor into HTML attributes, typing behaviour and accessible error messages.
column9: 1) The field components of #322 render the descriptor into HTML attributes (maxlength, min, max, step, pattern, accept, inputmode). 2) A small shared script shapes typing only (not a replacement for validation): normalise Persian/Arabic digits to ASCII, keep one decimal separator, cut decimals to the scale, show thousands separators without breaking RTL caret movement, strip disallowed characters. 3) Errors follow WCAG 2.2: text that identifies the field and says how to fix it (3.3.1, 3.3.3), not colour alone, aria-invalid on the field, message linked with aria-describedby, a summary with role alert, focus moved to the first invalid field. 4) Character counter and non-blocking hints. 5) No per-page script. 6) One shared JSON fixture file is run through the server validator and the script so both agree (parity test, see #361). Best-practice sources to apply: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (allowlist, syntactic and semantic checks, server-side authority, canonicalisation, limits before parsing, safe regular expressions); Microsoft Learn ASP.NET Core model validation; WCAG 2.2 success criteria 3.3.1 and 3.3.3; RFC 9457 problem details.
column10: Done when: a field built from metadata shows the right attributes and shapes typing for every type in the catalog; error text, aria attributes and focus pass an automated accessibility check (axe) and a screen-reader spot check; the parity fixtures pass on server and script; works in RTL and LTR.

column4: File and media field validation: per-field limits for size, total size, count, extensions, MIME with content check and image dimensions, aligned with the host request limit
column8: Request-size limits exist in 7 files without one source of truth, so the page, the application and the web host can disagree about the allowed size and the user sees a server error instead of a message. OWASP: treat file names and content types as untrusted; an allowed extension does not prove safe content.
column9: 1) Per-field settings: max size per file, max total size, max count, extension allowlist, MIME allowlist, image min/max width and height. 2) Server check on the upload pipeline of #183: size while streaming, extension, MIME and magic bytes (never trust the browser MIME), image dimensions, safe stored file name. 3) Derive the Kestrel/IIS request limit from the largest configured field limit (one setting in env/*.env) and show the same limit in the UI before upload. 4) Clear localised messages. 5) Per-entity or per-user quota hook.
column10: Done when: a file over the limit, with a wrong extension or a mismatching content type is rejected with a clear message at the UI and at the server; the host limit follows the setting; tests cover size boundary, wrong extension and a renamed file.

column4: Audit and harden validation of the existing static modules: string lengths, decimal precision and scale, numeric ranges, controllers without model validation, inputs without constraints, with a CI ratchet
column8: Validation in PEMS today is thin and scattered: 260 entities but only 26 [Required] and 45 [MaxLength] attributes in 28 files, no [Range], [StringLength] or regular-expression rule anywhere, no validation library, ModelState.IsValid is checked in 8 controllers, and 64 of 65 plain text inputs in the views have no maxlength. 136 decimal properties exist but only 110 precision mappings, and the application logs 'No store type was specified for the decimal property' at start (for example SparePart.QuantityOnHand, ReorderPoint, WorkOrder.DowntimeHours), which silently truncates values.
column9: 1) Write an audit script (extend tools/UiAudit or a test) listing: string properties without a maximum length or with nvarchar(max) that should be bounded; decimal properties without explicit precision and scale; numeric and date properties that need a range (quantities, percentages, years); controllers that write without ModelState or a validator; inputs in views without maxlength/min/max/step/inputmode. 2) Fix the highest-risk 30 first (money, quantities, identifiers, document numbers) with a migration where the column changes. 3) Add a test that fails when a new string property has no maximum length (unless marked unbounded) or a new decimal has no precision. 4) Report counts before and after in docs/audits.
column10: Done when: the audit report exists with counts; every decimal has explicit precision and the start-up warnings are gone; the 30 highest-risk fields are fixed; the ratchet test is in CI.

column4: Import and bulk paths use the same validation: row-level error report, partial-update semantics, defaults never NULL, malformed identifiers rejected as validation errors, size and row limits
column8: Import Center has 11 imports with their own checks. A blank cell in an update row must leave the value alone, a malformed identifier must never reach the database as a server error, and a default value must never be saved as NULL by a bulk path. 2026-10-28 plan audit: dependency/milestone corrected (see docs/audits/2026-10-28-dynamic-restful-audit.md).
column9: 1) The import designer (#25) and the Import Center call the validator of #356 per row. 2) Row-level error report (row, column, message, value) and a preview before commit. 3) Update mode: a blank cell leaves the stored value unchanged and 'required' applies only to columns present in the file. 4) Omitted columns with a default get the default (links to #26). 5) Reject malformed GUIDs and numeric keys as validation errors. 6) Limits for file size, rows and columns as settings (OWASP: cap sizes before parsing). 7) Persian digits and Jalali dates normalised (#364). 8) Test with 50,000 rows and mixed errors.
column10: Done when: a 50,000-row file with errors produces a complete row-level report and commits nothing, or only the valid rows if the user chooses; partial updates never clear data; a malformed identifier gives a message, not a server error.

column4: Validation test matrix and client/server parity suite: type by constraint by boundary, run on the server and in the browser script from the same fixtures
column8: A rule that the page and the server interpret differently is worse than no rule. No automated check exists today that proves they agree.
column9: 1) Data-driven fixtures: for each type and constraint the values min-1, min, max, max+1, zero, negative zero, very large numbers, scale+1, empty versus null versus whitespace, Persian and Arabic digits, mixed scripts, RTL marks and zero-width characters, characters outside the BMP counted by length. 2) Server test runs every fixture through the validator. 3) A browser-script test runs the same file through the client interpreter. 4) API-level tests prove a request that skips the UI is rejected. 5) CI runs both.
column10: Done when: the fixture file is the single source of truth, server and script give identical results for every case, and a deliberately broken rule fails the build.

column4: Field statistics endpoint and non-blocking hints: count, min, max, average, standard deviation and empty rate of a numeric field to suggest ranges in the designer and to flag unusual values on forms
column8: Choosing sensible min and max values blind is error-prone; the real data of the field is the best suggestion. Advisory hints must never block a save.
column9: 1) Endpoint returning count, min, max, average, standard deviation and empty rate for one numeric field, filtered by the central row-level security (#178) and cached. 2) Form designer shows the figures next to the range inputs and offers 'use observed range'. 3) The form shows a non-blocking 'unusual value' hint when a value is far from the average in units of the standard deviation. 4) Setting to turn hints off per field.
column10: Done when: the designer shows live statistics and can fill the range; an unusual value shows a hint but saves; a user cannot see statistics of records they cannot access.

column4: Validation error contract: RFC 9457 problem details with a list of field errors (pointer, constraint code, message key, parameters), the same shape for API, forms and import, with stable codes and error limits
column8: Each module reports errors in its own way (a page summary, a thrown message, a flash text), so clients and the form components cannot render or test them uniformly. RFC 9457 defines application/problem+json and leaves the validation list to an extension member; ASP.NET Core can produce problem details natively.
column9: 1) Define the response: status 400 or 422, type, title, detail and an 'errors' array where each item has field (JSON pointer), constraint code (for example min, max, maxLength, pattern, required, notUnique), message key, parameters and the localised text. 2) Implement it once (AddProblemDetails and an exception/validation filter) and use it for the generic engine, the API and import. 3) Stable constraint codes documented in the catalog (#355) so UI and tests depend on codes, not on text. 4) Settings for the maximum number of errors and the maximum nesting depth. 5) The form components of #357 and the import report of #360 render this one shape. 6) Never leak internal details, stack traces or SQL in the response.
column10: Done when: an invalid API call, form post and import row all return the same structured errors in the user's language; codes are stable and listed; a test fails if a module returns a different shape.

column4: Input canonicalisation and safe limits: one Unicode and Persian normalisation policy (digits, Arabic versus Persian letters, zero-width and bidi characters, trimming), whole-value regular expressions with timeout, and size/depth/count limits before parsing
column8: Persian text arrives with Arabic Yeh/Kaf instead of the Persian letters, Persian or Arabic digits, zero-width non-joiners and invisible bidi marks; without one policy the same name or code is stored in several forms, breaks uniqueness and search, and length checks count characters differently. OWASP: validate the canonical form, apply one normalisation policy before validation, storage and comparison, cap sizes before parsing, avoid regular expressions prone to catastrophic backtracking, treat a timeout as a failure.
column9: 1) Write the policy in the catalog (#355): Unicode NFC, Arabic Yeh/Kaf to Persian Yeh/Kaf, digits to ASCII for numbers and codes (keep the display digits as a presentation setting), trim and collapse spaces, remove or reject zero-width and bidi control characters except the zero-width non-joiner inside Persian words, per-field switch for exceptions. 2) Implement one normaliser used by the validator (#356), the import (#360) and the search; store the normalised form for unique keys and keep the original for display where needed. 3) Regular expressions: whole-value match, bounded input length, match timeout (the .NET regex timeout parameter or a non-backtracking engine), a failed timeout is a rejection. 4) Limits as settings: request body size, JSON nesting depth, array length, string length before any parsing. 5) Tests with Persian samples, look-alike characters and a catastrophic-backtracking pattern.
column10: Done when: the same Persian text typed with Arabic or Persian letters and digits is stored and compared as one value; a pattern that would backtrack catastrophically is stopped by the timeout; oversized or too deeply nested input is rejected before parsing; tests prove each case.

column4: Standards-based and local validators as a validator pack: e-mail and phone through maintained libraries, URL, Iranian national code, mobile number, postal code and IBAN (Sheba) checksum, valid Jalali dates, rial and toman scale
column8: Hand-written patterns for e-mail, phone and identifiers are the usual source of false rejections and of values that look valid but are not. OWASP: use a maintained library for e-mail and verify mailbox ownership separately; the local market also needs checksum rules (national code, IBAN mod 97) and Jalali calendar validity.
column9: 1) Check libraries first and record their licences (e-mail: the framework mail address parser; phone: a maintained E.164 library; IBAN: ISO 13616 mod-97). 2) Implement the Iranian rules as validators: ten-digit national code with its check digit, mobile number with accepted prefixes and normalisation to one stored form, postal code, economic code, legal-entity id. 3) Jalali date validity including leap years and conversion to the stored Gregorian date. 4) Currency fields: rial and toman scale, no floating point, decimal(18,2) style precision from #355. 5) Package them as a validator pack loaded through the extension SDK (#94) so other locales can add theirs. 6) Message keys in fa/en. 7) Tests with real valid and invalid samples.
column10: Done when: each validator accepts documented valid samples and rejects documented invalid ones, including checksum failures and non-existent Jalali dates; the pack loads through the extension point; e-mail and phone use a maintained library.

column4: Field format catalog: canonical storage form, display format, input format and parse rules per field type, presets, the settings hierarchy (system, app, model, field, user), label, help, placeholder, unit and empty-value formats, and the pipeline order with validation

Existing rows #24, #205, #206, #208 and #209 ask for translated labels, Persian digits, the Jalali calendar and fixed reports, but nothing defines where a field's format lives or how it relates to validation. A comparable implementation shows the risks: one hard-coded locale in its date component, date strings built without zero padding, an invalid-date defect in downloaded reports and a deprecated date library for the Jalali picker. 2026-10-28 plan audit: dependency/milestone corrected (see docs/audits/2026-10-28-dynamic-restful-audit.md).
column9: 1) For each type in #11 define three things: the canonical value that is stored and exchanged (ISO 8601 date-only for dates, UTC instant for date-times, decimal with fixed scale for numbers and money, normalised text), the display format, and the input and parse format. 2) Presets with examples (date: Jalali long/short, Gregorian ISO; number: grouping, decimal separator, digit shapes Latin or Persian; currency: rial, toman, symbol position, negative style; percent; units; boolean: yes/no, tick; empty value: dash). 3) Where a format lives: a settings hierarchy system -> app -> model -> field -> user preference with a defined fallback (a model or field setting wins for content, the user's setting for chrome), stored in the metadata registry as a versioned format object next to the validation object. 4) Label-related formats: label, help, placeholder, error and option text as translatable strings (#24), unit and prefix/suffix, direction. 5) State the pipeline order and the rule that validation always runs on the canonical value. 6) Write docs/architecture/FIELD_FORMAT_CATALOG.md and an ADR. Design rule (decided here, applies to #355-#365): formats and validations are designed together in one field descriptor and one test suite, but kept as separate layers of one pipeline: raw input -> parse by input format -> canonical value -> normalise (#364) -> validate the canonical value (#355/#356) -> store canonical -> format for display. Validation never runs on a display string, and a display format never changes what is stored. Best-practice sources: W3C Internationalization (date and number formats follow the language context, avoid ambiguous numeric dates, support non-Gregorian calendars, keep localisation separate from translation); MDN notes on input type=number (locale separators and non-ASCII digits are sanitised, no pattern support, so formatted or Persian input needs type=text with inputmode); ISO 8601 for stored dates; Unicode CLDR through Intl (browser) and ICU/CultureInfo (server); OWASP: validate the canonical form, one normalisation policy.

column4: First-run administrator setup: the administrator chooses the password in the UI as the last install step (fresh install, database reset, local dev, client server); the install is complete only after it
column8: Owner question 2026-10-27: how does the administrator get the first random password in the UI? Today the administrator comes from Seed__Admin__Password in the secrets file; nothing shows a generated password, and after a database reset the first-install flow must restart. 2026-10-27 owner decision: instead of generating, storing and revealing a random one-time password, the administrator sets the password in the UI as the last install step (no secret to generate or store, replaces the forced first change, uses the policy and the history rule of #382). This is the administrator step of the first-run wizard #169.
column9: 1) Condition: user table empty and no Seed__Admin__Password. Every request goes to /setup (static page) until done; staging and demo keep Seed__Admin__Password and skip it; an update never reaches it. 2) Guard against first-comer takeover: a one-time setup code written to a file next to the application and logged as a pointer only; /setup asks for it (optionally also server/management network only); rate limited; code and file deleted when the administrator exists; /setup is 404 afterwards. 3) Step: user name, e-mail, password (policy and history apply), confirm, sign in; MustChangePassword=false; the install is complete; licence/TLS/MFA steps of #169 attach to the same frame later. 4) After a database reset the page appears again with a new code. 5) Attempts go to Security Events (no password, no code). Two modes, decided only by whether Seed__Admin__Password is set: not set -> the administrator chooses the password on /setup, install complete, no forced change; set from an env/secrets file (staging, demo) -> the administrator is created from it and the first sign-in forces a change (MustChangePassword=true, history rule applies). An administrator password is never part of a client build.

column9: 1) Resource naming and URL rules (plural nouns, nested only for ownership, actions as POST sub-resources, e.g. POST /work-orders/{id}/actions/approve). 2) Verbs and status codes (200/201+Location/204/202, 400/401/403/404/409/412/422/428/429). 3) Query contract for paging, sorting, filtering, search, field selection (offset vs cursor decision). 4) Concurrency (ETag/If-Match, 412/428) and idempotency (Idempotency-Key). 5) Errors: RFC 9457 with the field-error list of #363. 6) Versioning and deprecation. 7) i18n: Accept-Language, TranslatableText JSON shape, UTC/ISO dates. 8) Allowed-actions and permission hints for dynamic UIs. 9) Browser auth (cookie plus antiforgery) vs integration auth (token). 10) Write the ADR and the guideline chapter.

column9: 1) Design first (small PR): one view helper and one script helper over IPemsLocale (number, integer, percent, decimal, date, date-time, count) with explicit raw escape hatch for attributes and values; decide how pages opt in (HtmlHelper or Tag Helper) and how scripts get the locale (data attribute). 2) Codemod the repeated patterns (ToString N0/N1/N3/0.###/0.0, yyyy-MM-dd, yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm) in waves by area with golden or render proof per wave (en byte-identical, fa digits only). 3) Scripts: replace toFixed and Intl.NumberFormat without a locale by the shared helper. 4) Ratchet test like the component raw-markup ratchet (#327): count of raw ToString format calls in views may only go down. 5) Exports (Excel, CSV, PDF) are covered by #371, not here. 6) Document in guideline chapter 02 what is display and what is data.
column10: Done when: a Persian user sees Persian digits in every displayed number and date on the migrated pages and in the scripts that draw numbers, an English user sees Latin digits exactly as today; links, ids, form values, CSV/Excel exports and API output stay Latin; a ratchet test fails when a view formats a number or date for display without the shared helper; every wave has before/after golden or render proof.
column11: Done in PR atapems-tech/PEMS#61 (merged): new IPemsLocale.Digits (digit swap, no reformatting; Format not used because it adds thousands separators); _PemsPagination shows Persian digits in the range text, page numbers and page-size buttons; hrefs and aria-labels stay Latin; English goldens byte-identical, 3 Persian goldens re-recorded and diffed (digits only).
